questions.text: Architect G's license expired December 31, 2025. In January 2026, she accepts design commission without renewal. She renews in February 2026. Violation:

options.text: No violation; renewed before substantial work
Practicing without current license
Fraud—misrepresenting licensure
Negligence in renewal timing

rationale.a: The timing of renewal is irrelevant. The violation occurs at the moment of accepting the work without a valid license. [cite: 540]
rationale.c: Fraud requires intentional misrepresentation. While practicing without a license is wrong, it does not necessarily constitute fraud unless the architect affirmatively misrepresented having a valid license. [cite: 538]
rationale.d: Negligence in timing mischaracterizes the violation. This is a regulatory violation for practicing architecture without a current license—a categorical prohibition. [cite: 540]
rationale.correct: Practicing without a current license is a regulatory violation; subsequent renewal does not cure the period of illegal practice. [cite: 540, 542]
rationale.takeaway: Practicing without current license is a non-negotiable violation. [cite: 542]

questions.text: Architect accepts medical facility commission without healthcare design experience or specialist engagement, violating standards. This pattern is:

options.text: Simple negligence, which may result in minor project delays or cost overruns
Incompetence and scope overreach
Fraud, which involves intentional deception for personal gain
Fiduciary breach, which occurs when the architect fails to act in the best interest of the client

rationale.a: Negligence alone does not capture the violation's severity. The issue is accepting a commission entirely outside the architect's competency—a categorical incompetence. [cite: 537]
rationale.c: Fraud requires intentional misrepresentation. While potentially deceptive, the specific professional violation is incompetence regarding technical scope. [cite: 538]
rationale.d: Fiduciary breach is too broad. The specific violation is incompetence and scope overreach under the standards requiring architects to maintain professional competency for accepted commissions. [cite: 537]
rationale.correct: Accepting work outside expertise without specialists is incompetence and scope overreach under RA 9266 Section 23. [cite: 525, 537]
rationale.takeaway: Architects must work within competency scope or engage specialists. [cite: 529]

questions.text: Architect F designs building and also designs contractor's temporary facility without developer knowledge. Contractor's equipment storage reduces developer's staging area. Violation is:

options.text: Negligence in site planning, which involves failing to consider the impact of temporary facilities on the overall project layout and developer's needs
Undisclosed conflict of interest
Fraud in concealing relationship, which could involve intentionally hiding the dual role to gain personal advantage or benefit the contractor
Fiduciary breach, as it involves a failure to act in the best interest of the developer by prioritizing the contractor's needs

rationale.a: The fundamental violation is the undisclosed conflict. Negligence describes poor execution; the real issue is divided loyalty without transparency. [cite: 632, 644]
rationale.c: The omission constitutes an undisclosed conflict of interest, which is a sufficient violation without requiring proof of fraudulent intent. [cite: 532, 538]
rationale.d: Fiduciary breach is broader. The specific violation under ethics standards is an undisclosed conflict affecting professional standing. [cite: 532, 633]
rationale.correct: Serving multiple parties with conflicting interests without disclosure violates SPP 200 Article III Section 4.9. [cite: 521, 532]
rationale.takeaway: Conflicts with opposed parties require full disclosure and written consent. [cite: 589, 629]

questions.text: Architect C certifies design code compliance without detailed review due to time constraints, found later to violate code in three areas. PRBoA characterizes this as:

options.text: Negligence, as it involves a failure to exercise the care that a reasonably prudent architect would exercise in similar circumstances
Fraud—false certification without actual review
Incompetence, reflecting a lack of ability, knowledge, or qualification to perform architectural duties
Regulatory violation only, which does not necessarily imply intent or negligence but still breaches professional standards

rationale.a: Negligence describes careless conduct. Signing a certification of code compliance without performing the review is an affirmative false statement—fraud. [cite: 601]
rationale.c: Incompetence refers to lack of ability. The architect chose to skip the review due to time, making this intentional falsification rather than a lack of knowledge. [cite: 538]
rationale.d: Characterizing this as merely a regulatory violation understates the conduct. It is an ethical and moral violation (fraud) beyond regulatory noncompliance. [cite: 538]
rationale.correct: Signing certification without actual review constitutes intentional misrepresentation (fraud) under RA 9266 Section 23. [cite: 538, 601]
rationale.takeaway: False compliance certification is a ground for revocation. [cite: 538]

questions.text: Architects H and I both committed code violations. H discovered mid-project, corrected, informed client, completed successfully. I's error discovered post-occupancy by inspector. PRBoA likely:

options.text: Identical discipline for same violation, which is unlikely given the circumstances
H lighter discipline for proactive correction; I harsher discipline
I lighter discipline; didn't discover error, which is not typically how discipline is assessed
Both severe due to public safety risk, which may not consider proactive correction

rationale.a: PRBoA calibrates discipline based on aggravating and mitigating factors, including the architect's conduct post-discovery. [cite: 542, 602]
rationale.c: Failing to discover an error before occupancy reflects inadequate oversight. H's proactive approach is a mitigating factor, not I's passivity an excuse. [cite: 543, 811]
rationale.d: While safety risk is severe, H's prompt correction reduces professional culpability compared to I's failure that persisted into occupancy. [cite: 542, 796]
rationale.correct: PRBoA considers prompt discovery and remediation (mitigation) when determining the severity of discipline. [cite: 542, 607]
rationale.takeaway: Proactive correction is a significant mitigating factor in disciplinary proceedings. [cite: 607]

questions.text: Architect negligently designed system causing $500,000 damage. Architect settles with client for $250,000. PRBoA restitution order will be:

options.text: Limited to $250,000 settlement
Based on full $500,000 harm
No restitution due to settlement
Reduced for architect's good faith settlement

rationale.a: Private settlements do not constrain PRBoA authority. The board's role is to address the professional violation and its full impact. [cite: 542]
rationale.c: A private settlement does not eliminate the authority to order restitution as part of professional discipline for public interest. [cite: 542]
rationale.d: Restitution is based on the actual loss established by quantifiable damages, not on mitigation efforts during settlement. [cite: 795, 798]
rationale.correct: PRBoA restitution reflects the actual harm caused by negligence, not private civil settlements. [cite: 542, 798]
rationale.takeaway: Disciplinary restitution reflects full harm regardless of private settlement amounts. [cite: 542, 606]

questions.text: Architect A designs a residential building with 3.5 kPa floor load capacity but submits permit with 5 kPa specification. During construction, noticing the discrepancy but assuming contractor will comply with lower spec, the building later deflects. This violation is:

options.text: Contractor's responsibility only, as they are expected to verify all specifications before proceeding with construction
Architect's negligence for failing to correct discovered error
Fraud because false specs were submitted, misleading the contractor and potentially endangering the structure
Architect not at fault, as the responsibility lies solely with the contractor to ensure compliance with all specifications

rationale.a: While contractor responsibility exists, the architect has a duty to correct errors in plans; failing to do so makes the architect liable for negligence. [cite: 790]
rationale.c: Fraud requires intentional misrepresentation. Without evidence of intentional falsification for gain, this is a negligent omission rather than fraud. [cite: 538]
rationale.d: The architect is at fault. Failing to issue a correction for a discovered discrepancy is a negligent omission that directly compromises structural safety. [cite: 789, 794]
rationale.correct: The architect observed a discrepancy but failed to issue a correction—this constitutes negligence in professional duty. [cite: 786, 796]
rationale.takeaway: Architects must correct design discrepancies they discover in construction documents. [cite: 803]

questions.text: Architect E observes missing required firestop systems during CA, documents in report but issues no formal non-compliance notice. PRBoA will find:

options.text: Not liable; contractor responsible
Negligent for failing to enforce compliance
Not responsible; contractor obligation only
Contractor violation absolves architect

rationale.a: Documentation in a report does not satisfy the duty to the client. The CA obligation includes actively enforcing compliance, not merely noting violations. [cite: 742, 839]
rationale.c: Architects cannot abdicate their duty to ensure code compliance during CA. This is a primary professional obligation to public welfare. [cite: 515, 543]
rationale.d: A contractor's violation does not absolve the architect. The failure to demand correction is an independent negligent act. [cite: 814, 816]
rationale.correct: Architect must actively enforce code compliance during CA; documentation alone is insufficient oversight. [cite: 710, 839]
rationale.takeaway: Architects must enforce code compliance during Construction Administration. [cite: 543]

questions.text: Architect D receives 12% commission from glazing supplier, discloses to clients who accept in writing. This conduct is:

options.text: Unprofessional—any commission is conflict
Professional if disclosed and consented
Permitted under the 2010 SPP 208 code
Professional because architect ensures objectivity

rationale.b: Disclosure and consent cannot override the categorical prohibition in SPP Doc 200. The code prohibits these returns absolutely to maintain professional impartiality. [cite: 589, 641]
rationale.c: SPP 208 covers Design Competitions and does not grant permission for commissions. SPP 200 is the governing document for this ethical conduct. [cite: 517, 824]
rationale.d: Subjective objectivity is irrelevant. The code prohibits the relationship because it creates inherent conflicts of economic interest. [cite: 641, 644]
rationale.correct: SPP Document 200 (Article III, Section 4.6 and Article V, Section 6.1) categorically prohibits accepting commissions from suppliers or interested parties. The acceptance itself is the violation, regardless of disclosure.
rationale.takeaway: Architect commissions from suppliers are strictly prohibited regardless of transparency. [cite: 550, 644]

questions.text: Architect J: 2-year suspension for inadequate site investigation completed. Now faces identical complaint on new project. Effect of prior violation:

options.text: No effect; discipline paid, and the architect is free to continue practice without additional penalties.
Repeat offender status—aggravating factor supporting harsher discipline
Automatic revocation, as repeated violations indicate a pattern of negligence that cannot be overlooked.
Automatic probation, allowing the architect to continue practice under strict supervision to prevent further violations.

rationale.a: Prior violations remain part of the professional record and inform subsequent disciplinary assessments. [cite: 542]
rationale.c: While not 'automatic,' the prior suspension significantly increases the likelihood of revocation if the pattern continues. [cite: 525]
rationale.d: Aggravating factors typically push discipline toward suspension or revocation rather than lighter probation. [cite: 602]
rationale.correct: A prior similar violation is an aggravating factor that justifies harsher discipline (potentially revocation) for repeat offenses. [cite: 525, 542]
rationale.takeaway: Patterns of professional failure lead to escalating disciplinary consequences. [cite: 542, 602]
